note: 5,172 support agents, 15 percent productivity gain concentrated in less experienced workers, the most cited field study of AI at work.
title: Generative AI at Work

reading.body:
The largest field study of AI at work found a 15 percent productivity gain for customer service agents, concentrated entirely among inexperienced workers, suggesting the technology transfers knowledge rather than replacing skill.

A conversational AI system deployed to 5,172 support agents produced measurable gains in issues resolved per hour. The effect was not uniform. Newer agents improved substantially while experienced workers saw negligible gains. This pattern indicates the AI functioned as a knowledge transfer mechanism, surfacing solutions that skilled workers had developed through years of practice and making them available to workers still building expertise.

The implication for AI scaling is indirect but significant. If AI's primary value in knowledge work is accelerating junior worker productivity, then expanding AI deployment depends not on replacing experienced staff but on growing the workforce to absorb that productivity gain. This creates a binding constraint different from compute or power: the availability of trainable labor. The data does not address whether the same gains persist as junior workers accumulate experience, or whether the AI becomes less valuable as the workforce matures.

The study also notes secondary effects on customer satisfaction and employee retention, which affect labor supply but lie outside the measured productivity metric. The data covers one function at one company at one moment in time and does not establish whether these results generalize across sectors, skill distributions, or types of knowledge work.

explain_beginner: This study asks a very concrete version of a big question, does giving workers access to a generative AI assistant actually make them more productive on the job, measured in a real workplace rather than a lab. The researchers studied a large software company's customer support operation, where thousands of agents, most of them based in the Philippines, handle live chats with customers, and where the company rolled out a GPT based tool that suggests responses to agents in real time as they type. Because the tool was rolled out to different teams at different times, the researchers could compare agents who had it against similar agents who did not yet have it, holding time and individual differences roughly constant. What they found is that access to the AI assistant raised the number of issues resolved per hour, but the gain was extremely uneven, brand new agents improved dramatically while the most experienced agents barely changed. It does not tell us whether these gains hold up over years, whether they change how many agents a company needs to hire, or whether wages eventually rise to reflect the higher output, because the study window was too short to observe any of that.
explain_business: For any company running a large customer service or similar structured knowledge work operation, the actionable takeaway is that generative AI assistants deliver their biggest and most measurable return on newer and lower performing staff, not on your best people, which should directly shape where a pilot program is targeted and how its success is measured. A rollout evaluated only on average productivity gains, roughly 14 percent here, would understate the tool's effect on ramping new hires and understate that senior staff may see little direct benefit from the same deployment. The cost side is that this was a build, not a buy, the company constructed a purpose built tool trained on its own best agent conversations, so the 14 to 34 percent figures are not guaranteed to transfer to an off the shelf chatbot plugged into an unrelated workflow. This applies now to any structured, high volume text based service role, and the open question this study leaves for a business to answer on its own is whether faster ramping of new hires should change hiring plans, training budget, or headcount, since the paper itself does not extend far enough in time to say.
explain_practitioner: Using data from roughly 5,179 customer support agents and about 3 million chat conversations, the authors exploit a staggered rollout of an internal GPT based assistant to estimate causal effects with a difference in differences design, comparing treated and not yet treated agents over time. The average effect was a 14 percent increase in issues resolved per hour, driven by shorter average handling time and the ability to manage more simultaneous chats, with resolution rates and customer satisfaction essentially flat. The distribution behind that average masked a much sharper pattern, novice and lower skilled agents gained roughly 34 percent, while the most tenured, highest performing agents saw little to no measurable improvement, and treated agents with about two months of tenure performed on par with untreated agents who had six months of experience. That compression toward the top performer's skill level, rather than a uniform boost, is the paper's central empirical result, and it argues the tool functions partly as a channel for transferring the practices of the best agents to everyone else. The authors are explicit that their design cannot speak to longer run effects on staffing levels, wages, or whether these gains persist once agents fully adapt, since the observation window covers only a few months after rollout.
